COMMIT 7027ffa32fb9eab60d909d500c307dc384d4ec51 fix(telemetry): only announce skill events the outermost frame saved
fix(telemetry): only announce skill events the outermost frame saved

MutateSessionStateSaved reported saved=true for a nested frame on the
grounds that the outer frame flushes its mutations. That is a prediction,
not a fact: if the outer frame then returns ErrMutationSkip or fails, the
caller has already emitted telemetry for an append that never reached
disk.

For skill events that is not self-correcting. Extraction re-derives from
transcript offset 0 on every pass and dedupes against the ledger in
session state, so an event whose ledger entry never landed is re-derived
by the next pass, returned as new, and announced a second time —
duplicating it in PostHog, which is exactly what the ledger exists to
prevent.

Replace the bool with MutateSessionStateOnSaved(ctx, id, fn, onSaved):
the caller hands over the effect and the helper runs it from the only
frame that knows whether a save happened. Nested registrations queue on
the session gate; the outermost frame drains them after its own save
succeeds and discards them when it skips or fails. Effects still run
after release(), so the settings load and detached spawn never extend
the gate hold.

No behavior change today — every current call site is outermost, so the
nested branch was unreachable. It stops being a landmine for the next
refactor that moves one of these handlers under a gate.

Also updates the three contract doc comments (skill_events,
skill_telemetry, telemetry_signals) that told callers to emit "after the
surrounding MutateSessionState returns" to name the new helper.

Tests: the nested contract as a table (outer saves / skips / fails),
asserting the effect never runs while the outer frame is open, that a
skipped outer frame leaves nothing on disk, and that a queued effect
does not leak into the next frame on the same session. Each case fails
against the old nested behavior.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

END
COMMIT 39d1bfe00bcffb8686fe9d8d595758d0dddb1724 review: commit-scope the payload, gate the scan, sanitize the matcher
review: commit-scope the payload, gate the scan, sanitize the matcher

Six confirmed findings from the pre-review pass:

- The search probe is now computed at exactly one choke point
  (CondenseSession), so the interrupted-condensation recovery result carries
  it like every other path and no future extractor branch can ship the
  zero-value probe by omission. The three per-branch assignments are gone.

- The scan is gated BEFORE it runs: condensation consults the emitter's
  memoized telemetry gate (condenseOpts.searchProbeAllowed), so opted-out and
  not-opted-in users never pay the full-transcript pass, and the two
  never-emitting condensation paths (doctor repair, session-end leftovers)
  never scan at all.

- files_committed and prior_ai_history are commit-scoped by construction:
  newCommitCondensedSignal re-intersects FilesTouched against the commit's
  file set, so the one upstream path that deliberately does not narrow
  (filterFilesTouched on an empty committed set — --allow-empty, failed file
  detection) can no longer count a session's uncommitted files.

- The command matcher no longer reads separators inside quoted arguments or
  heredoc bodies as command boundaries: sanitizeShellCommandForMatching
  blanks those spans (removal-only, so the hint-prefilter contract holds by
  construction) before the position regex runs. `git commit -m "wip; entire
  search notes"`, `rg "foo|entire search bar"`, and a heredoc writing the
  search skill's own body no longer count as invocations.

- The prior-history probe is anchored: it walks git log from the explicit
  commit hash PostCommit is reporting on (HEAD can move before the post-gate
  probe runs) and scrubs the GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE that git exports to hooks,
  via gitEnvWithoutRepoOverrides like this package's other `git -C` call.

- The entire-search subagent name is one exported constant
  (strategy.EntireSearchSubagentName): the installer scaffolds its paths from
  it and a new test pins the template bodies to it, so a rename fails a test
  instead of silently zeroing used_search_source="subagent".

Also aligns the payload docs with the deliberate scoping split (used_search
is session-scoped, the other properties commit-scoped) and fixes the stale
"Cursor can never be probed" test comment that contradicted
agent/tool_invocations.go. resolveShadowRefAndTree is extracted from
postCommitProcessSessionLocked, which the new emitter parameter had pushed
past the maintidx threshold.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

COMMIT a8189812520ddc07cc646493b900dc5f3883d501 review: probe prior AI history once per commit, and anchor its parse on NUL
review: probe prior AI history once per commit, and anchor its parse on NUL

Three findings on the same function, landed together because each part
would otherwise be written twice: the hoist changes its signature, and
the format fix rewrites the body it returns.

Per-session probe -> per-commit (MEDIUM). emitCommitCondensedTelemetry
ran inside PostCommit's per-session loop and each call shelled out to
`git log -z --skip=1 -n 50 --name-only`. Measured p50 of 25 runs: 13.8ms
for the probe, and 8.7ms for `git --version` alone -- so roughly 9ms of
it is process startup, and the timing is flat across a 60x range of
output size (4.8KB to 133KB). The walk is nearly free; the process is the
cost. Since the output is commit-scoped and identical for every session
in the commit -- only the per-session intersection differs -- paying it
per session was paying for spawns.

So priorAICommitTouchedFiles (predicate) becomes priorAICommitFiles
(set), and commitCondensedEmitter memoizes both the scan and the
settings load for one commit. Constructed once in PostCommit from the
worktreePath already in scope, which also drops the per-session
paths.WorktreeRoot call and its error branch.

Memoization is not the gate. Both halves resolve on FIRST USE, and the
order inside emit is the promise the doc comment already made: a commit
where no session condenses runs neither settings.Load nor git log, and an
opted-out user never reaches the probe. Two tests pin that rather than
trusting the reading -- a nil signal must not even resolve the gate, and
an opted-out user (explicitly, and with the key absent, since telemetry
is opt-in) must see zero probe calls. Plain flags rather than sync.Once
because the loop is sequential and the struct's other state is unguarded
anyway; that constraint is stated on the type.

Don't oversell the settings half: settings.Load is uncached and already
called several times per hook process elsewhere (see the OPF note in
CLAUDE.md). This memoizes one hook, it does not fix that pattern.

Telemetry gate idiom (LOW). The hand-rolled `s.Telemetry == nil ||
!*s.Telemetry` is gone; allowed() calls s.IsTelemetryEnabled(), the
helper #2023 extracted precisely to stop this being copied a fourth time.
The load is retained because s.Enabled is still needed at send time. Also
adds the emitCommitCondensed send seam, matching emitSkillTelemetry, so
the gate is testable without a PostHog client.

Unescaped git-log format (LOW). `--format=%x1e%B%x1f` took both
delimiters from the raw body, so a commit message containing either
control character split a record early -- dropping the real
Entire-Checkpoint trailer with it. Verified against git 2.53.0: the old
format on such a commit yields a record whose message is " and ", whose
trailer is absent, and whose "file list" is the rest of the message. That
makes prior_ai_history read false, which suppresses a genuine miss. Same
failure direction as the used_search finding, which is why it is worth
fixing properly rather than narrowing.

Replaced with `--format=%x00%H%n%B`. -z NUL-terminates the format output
itself and a commit message cannot contain NUL, so splitting the whole
output on NUL makes an empty field an unambiguous record marker -- one
that rests on nothing about message content. %H earns its four characters
by guaranteeing the post-marker field is non-empty, so an empty-message
commit cannot emit two adjacent markers and mis-frame the record after
it; TestPriorAICommitFiles_EmptyMessageCommit pins that, and the hash is
a free debugging anchor. trailers.ParseCheckpoint stays the single
definition of what a checkpoint trailer is, and its regex is unanchored,
so the leading hash line is inert.

Rejected %(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly), which would keep
the body out of the output entirely, on semantics rather than
compatibility. It hands trailer detection to git's parser, which only
recognises a trailer block in the message's final paragraph, while
trailers.ParseCheckpoint matches anywhere. Commits whose trailer is not
last-paragraph -- reworded commits, hand-edited squash bodies, and the
multi-trailer squash-merge case ParseAllCheckpoints exists for -- would
newly be missed, and the divergence would be invisible in the data.
Keeping %B also keeps trailers.ParseCheckpoint as the single definition
of what a checkpoint trailer is, which is worth more here than the
narrower injection surface. (The placeholder also predates git 2.15, but
that is 2017 and not a real constraint; the semantics are the reason.)

Rejected a two-pass
hashes-then-names design outright: spawns are the cost, per above.

Merge commits still contribute nothing, and the reasoning is now recorded
on the function instead of being implicit. --name-only emits no names for
a merge, and the obvious fix (--diff-merges=first-parent) would make a
"Merge origin/main into X" commit attribute every file it merged in,
inflating prior_ai_history and therefore the miss rate. A merge's content
is already attributed to the individual trailer-carrying commits it
brings in, which are in this window on their own account -- 51 of the
last 300 merges on main carry the trailer, so this is a frequent path,
not a rare one. Squash merges are single-parent, so their files do appear.
TestPriorAICommitFiles_MergeCommitContributesNothing pins the decision so
a future "fix" has to argue with a test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

END
COMMIT 4702ab415cc748a5df3e8a9c3003cb41ddb3f776 refactor(telemetry): name the event for the commit it describes

cli_checkpoint_condensed promises "a checkpoint was condensed" and
delivers "a commit condensed a checkpoint". That gap already produced a
HIGH review finding reading the absent emission on the doctor and
session-end condensation paths as data loss, and it would mislead anyone
querying total condensations.

Renaming is free exactly now: this PR is unmerged, so the event has never
been emitted in a release and no dashboard keys on it. After it ships it
stops being free.

caller is condenseAndUpdateState via postCommitProcessSessionLocked, and
folding in the commit-less paths would add rows indistinguishable from
genuine misses — inflating the denominator rather than completing it.

commit-scoped fields), not a bug fix.

COMMIT 165a27c2d50c7df2706ed48e88fc465dd0bb3084 Keep a plugin's own output inside the warning it belongs to
Keep a plugin's own output inside the warning it belongs to

A failed removal's reason is the plugin's stderr, which is arbitrary text
and often several lines. Printed as one Fprintf, every line after the first
started at column zero and read as a new top-level message, exactly where
the user is being told what is still installed on their machine. Warnings
now indent continuation lines past the marker.

The progress line grew a dot per second, so a slow plugin eventually wrapped
and the single-row erase left the earlier rows on screen. Redraw a fixed
"(Ns)" counter in place instead, which also answers how long it has been
waiting. Its teardown is deferred so a panic cannot strand the ticker
goroutine and half a line.

Name the removed agent the same way the failure lines do, via
agentDisplayName, so an unresolvable name cannot render differently
depending on whether its removal worked.

COMMIT bd7fab04431e283c4e4f4cfdf0874a701efe0017 Say what uninstall really does with an agent it could not check
Say what uninstall really does with an agent it could not check

Three comments claimed an unchecked agent's hooks get removed in-process
if it is built-in. They do not: a failed check is not a licence to rewrite
that agent's config, since whatever broke the read is the same thing a
removal would have to parse. The behaviour is right; the comments were
describing a design that was considered and dropped, which is worse than
no comment at all for the next person deciding whether to "fix" it.

Also document the contract this puts on plugin authors, which existed only
in the CLI's code until now: are-hooks-installed failing means "unknown",
not "no hooks", and uninstall-hooks failing fails the whole command and
gets the plugin's stderr shown to the user verbatim.

COMMIT 3cca76f40b5bd02b001337112055b4d487eeb510 Drop --strict: any failed uninstall step now fails the command
Drop --strict: any failed uninstall step now fails the command

The uninstall had two verdicts for the same facts: a leftover external
plugin's hooks warned but exited 0 unless the caller opted into --strict.
Now there is one contract — any step that fails (built-in agent, external
plugin, git hooks, session states, .entire/, shadow branches) exits
non-zero with a did-not-complete verdict.

Consequences:
- The 'not installed' short-circuit requires every agent to be checked:
  an unchecked plugin falls through, gets warned about with both
  remedies, and fails the run — closing the re-run hole where an
  unprobeable plugin as the only leftover silently claimed 'not
  installed' (trail finding 01M0YZ88ZY1V).
- A failed external removal prints both remedies: re-run (discovery is
  ungated) and the direct plugin command (the plugin binary may be what
  is broken).
- Known tradeoff: a broken entire-agent-* binary anywhere on $PATH now
  fails uninstall in every repo until fixed or removed.

Also make every step's failure render like the agent step: red ✗
headline naming the step, reason nested beneath it — and stop
double-wrapping the .entire/ and session-state errors that made the
warning read 'failed to remove X: failed to remove X: ...'.

item.stdout:
LINE 9: Windows replacement contention is handled inside `jsonutil` rather than OpenCode. Only access-denied and sharing-violation failures are retried, with five total attempts and cancellation-aware waits. The follow-up review found a cancellation window between retries: cancellation could occur after a wait, but the next rename could still replace the destination. The retry loop now checks the context before every rename attempt, retaining the validated staging file if cancellation wins.

OpenCode continues to translate publication failures into its existing actionable “export saved at …” message. Its package-specific staging, rename, and contention helpers have been removed because those responsibilities now belong to the shared atomic-write implementation.

## API Notes

This adds the public `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicStream` helper and the public `jsonutil.PublishError` ownership contract. A caller receiving `PublishError` owns the validated file at `StagedPath` and must either recover or remove it.

LINE 7: Follow-up to #2046 and #2047, clearing the seven review findings left open on trails #1088 and #1089. No new behaviour — this is the cleanup those two PRs deferred, plus one real narrowing they introduced.

## What changed

**The not-onboarded line (the only string a user in a non-onboarded repo sees)**

It was anonymous *and* overconfident. It printed "This repository" even for `--repo gh/other/thing`, where the failing repo isn't the current clone — and since the branch returns a `SilentError`, the chain that *did* name the repo never printed, so nothing identified it at all. It also asserted a missing mirror, while `errRepoNotOnboarded` covers three shapes and only one is really "not onboarded": zero rows also means the caller cannot **see** the repo (where `entire repo mirror create` would fail too), and a row with no processing primary can be mid-onboarding.

LINE 28: ## Known gaps / follow-ups

1. ~~**Pre-existing orphan-prune gap.**~~ **Fixed by #2032.** `findSessionsForWorktree`'s orphan sweep now spares record-bearing sessions (`!state.HasTaskContent()` in the prune predicate), so an idle session whose only activity is one open task record survives to `prepare-commit-msg` — a first-turn background commit links. The integration test's read-only seed-task workaround has been removed accordingly.
2. ~~**Sweep-finalize follow-up.**~~ **Fixed by #2032.** `finalizeExitedSessions` now completes a dead-owner session's live records (`sweepCompleteLiveTaskRecords`, `session_finalize.go`) before ending it, exactly as a clean SessionEnd does — preserving transcripts and closing the trust-window trade-off from the other end.
3. **Identity/ancestry discovery** (linking a commit to a session by content/authorship signals beyond records) composes into the same fast-path loop later, via #2013. Out of scope here.

## Trailer eligibility is bounded; condensability is not

---
LINE 31: 2. ~~**Sweep-finalize follow-up.**~~ **Fixed by #2032.** `finalizeExitedSessions` now completes a dead-owner session's live records (`sweepCompleteLiveTaskRecords`, `session_finalize.go`) before ending it, exactly as a clean SessionEnd does — preserving transcripts and closing the trust-window trade-off from the other end.
3. **Identity/ancestry discovery** (linking a commit to a session by content/authorship signals beyond records) composes into the same fast-path loop later, via #2013. Out of scope here.

## Trailer eligibility is bounded; condensability is not

A session's task records make it condensable with no freshness bound — that is deliberate, and it is what keeps a stale record's transcript-so-far from being stranded unmaterialized. Claiming a commit is bounded separately: only a record within `idleWithTaskContent`'s 24h window may mint a trailer. Without that split, an IDLE session whose only content was a >24h record got a trailer from the slow path and was then refused by PostCommit, leaving `Entire-Checkpoint` pointing at a checkpoint nothing ever wrote — on an unrelated human commit. Two reviewers reproduced it end to end; `staleRecordIsOnlyContent` closes it, and PostCommit now warns whenever a trailer is minted and no session condenses into it, so any future divergence is visible rather than silent.

An earlier revision of this PR also exempted record-bearing sessions from PostCommit's read-only skip. That is reverted: the skip only fires when another session's files are in the commit, and PostCommit hands one checkpoint ID to every condensing session, so that other session fills the trailer anyway. The exemption prevented no dangling trailer and only let a record-bearing session condense into someone else's commit.

Claiming a commit is bounded separately: only a record within `idleWithTaskContent`'s 24h window may mint a trailer. Without that split, an IDLE session whose only content was a >24h record got a trailer from the slow path and was then refused by PostCommit, leaving `Entire-Checkpoint` pointing at a checkpoint nothing ever wrote — on an unrelated human commit. Two reviewers reproduced it end to end; `staleRecordIsOnlyContent` closes it, and PostCommit now warns whenever a trailer is minted and no session condenses into it, so any future divergence is visible rather than silent.

An earlier revision of this PR also exempted record-bearing sessions from PostCommit's read-only skip. That is reverted: the skip only fires when another session's files are in the commit, and PostCommit hands one checkpoint ID to every condensing session, so that other session fills the trailer anyway. The exemption prevented no dangling trailer and only let a record-bearing session condense into someone else's commit.

item.stdout:
LINE 15: `CondensationRecoveryPending` separately records when recovery may need to reconcile an interrupted write created by an older CLI version. This keeps the more expensive storage lookup out of normal condensation paths.

Reserved writes are routed using their checkpoint ID format. If checkpoint configuration changes between reservation and retry, the checkpoint is still written to the backend that originally generated its ID.

### Recovering state from older CLI versions

Older interrupted sessions have no pending checkpoint ID. Doctor reconciles them using the session identity, transcript bounds and content, checkpoint counts, agent and turn metadata, touched files, and session kind. Externalized images are reinserted before comparing transcripts.

---
LINE 31: ### Follow-up plan

This PR lands the non-destructive part first: it prevents new duplicate checkpoints, makes retries deterministic, and reconciles interrupted writes from older CLI versions. It deliberately does not remove or hide duplicate pairs that already exist.

Questions for a follow-up:

1. Should existing duplicate pairs remain as physical history and be collapsed only in `checkpoint list` and `tokens profile`, or should `doctor` repair the stored history?
2. If one checkpoint becomes canonical, which should win: the original session-end write or the later recovery write? What should happen when their metadata differs?
---
LINE 35: Questions for a follow-up:

1. Should existing duplicate pairs remain as physical history and be collapsed only in `checkpoint list` and `tokens profile`, or should `doctor` repair the stored history?
2. If one checkpoint becomes canonical, which should win: the original session-end write or the later recovery write? What should happen when their metadata differs?
3. Should repair be automatic, an explicit doctor action, or reporting-only until the user chooses?
4. Should transcript-range idempotency become a shared rule for every condensation entry point, or remain limited to session-end and doctor recovery?

Once those product choices are clear, existing duplicates can be handled separately without coupling destructive cleanup or changed read semantics to this durability fix.

3. **Identity/ancestry discovery** (linking a commit to a session by content/authorship signals beyond records) composes into the same fast-path loop later, via #2013. Out of scope here.

## Trailer eligibility is bounded; condensability is not

A session's task records make it condensable with no freshness bound — that is deliberate, and it is what keeps a stale record's transcript-so-far from being stranded unmaterialized. Claiming a commit is bounded separately: only a record within `idleWithTaskContent`'s 24h window may mint a trailer. Without that split, an IDLE session whose only content was a >24h record got a trailer from the slow path and was then refused by PostCommit, leaving `Entire-Checkpoint` pointing at a checkpoint nothing ever wrote — on an unrelated human commit. Two reviewers reproduced it end to end; `staleRecordIsOnlyContent` closes it, and PostCommit now warns whenever a trailer is minted and no session condenses into it, so any future divergence is visible rather than silent.

An earlier revision of this PR also exempted record-bearing sessions from PostCommit's read-only skip. That is reverted: the skip only fires when another session's files are in the commit, and PostCommit hands one checkpoint ID to every condensing session, so that other session fills the trailer anyway. The exemption prevented no dangling trailer and only let a record-bearing session condense into someone else's commit.

#2053
LINE 9: Windows replacement contention is handled inside `jsonutil` rather than OpenCode. Only access-denied and sharing-violation failures are retried, with five total attempts and cancellation-aware waits. The follow-up review found a cancellation window between retries: cancellation could occur after a wait, but the next rename could still replace the destination. The retry loop now checks the context before every rename attempt, retaining the validated staging file if cancellation wins.

OpenCode continues to translate publication failures into its existing actionable “export saved at …” message. Its package-specific staging, rename, and contention helpers have been removed because those responsibilities now belong to the shared atomic-write implementation.

## API Notes

This adds the public `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicStream` helper and the public `jsonutil.PublishError` ownership contract. A caller receiving `PublishError` owns the validated file at `StagedPath` and must either recover or remove it.

{"body":"Refs #2091, item 3 only.

Before this change, Claude Code's Stop hook waited for a transcript sentinel that no longer appears, then fell back to a 500 ms quiet window. The wait only validated a mutable path. Lifecycle copied that path later, and provisional-checkpoint finalization opened it once more. Entire could therefore store bytes other than the ones it had treated as ready.

This PR replaces that sequence with one owned, validated snapshot for Claude Stop. Modern Claude payloads provide the final assistant response, so Entire can validate a transcript immediately with no artificial wait. Older payloads retain the 500 ms quiet-window fallback. The lifecycle also keeps checkpoints refreshable across Claude's repeatable Stop events and derives file and token metadata from one transcript parse.

## The wait did not own the transcript

TranscriptPreparer returns only an error. It gives the caller no bytes, open handle, identity, size, or file version. A successful wait says that path state A looked ready, but lifecycle can then copy state B and checkpoint finalization can read state C.

Shortening the wait alone would reduce latency while leaving that race intact. Valid final JSON would not be enough either: a complete older prefix can be syntactically valid even when the current turn has not reached the file.

## Owned, validated Stop snapshots

The built-in Claude Code adapter now has a Stop-specific capture operation. It:

1. fingerprints the producer-owned transcript by file identity, size, and modification time;
2. reads exactly the observed byte range;
3. verifies both the opened handle and current path still identify the observed file version;
4. validates the JSONL and derives the position from those exact bytes; and
5. returns an Entire-owned snapshot used by lifecycle, metadata analysis, position advancement, and checkpoint finalization.

None of those consumers reopens Claude's live transcript for the same Stop. If the file changes during capture, the bytes are discarded and capture retries against the new version.

The portable fingerprint catches ordinary appends, truncation, replacement, and rewrites whose modification time changes. It cannot prove that a same-size rewrite did not happen when the filesystem also reports the same timestamp. Claude appends transcript records, so that is an acceptable limit here; the tests do not claim stronger detection.

## Modern readiness is evidence-based and immediate

For modern payloads, non-empty last_assistant_message supplies current-turn evidence. Capture requires a transcript position successfully measured at TurnStart, reconstructs the latest assistant text only after that boundary, and requires it to match Claude's supplied final response.

The first readiness check now runs immediately. The previous design waited for the first 50 ms ticker event even when the transcript was already complete. After the immediate attempt, incomplete captures return to the normal 50 ms polling cadence.

A rejected file fingerprint is remembered. Entire does not reread and revalidate the same unchanged 70 MiB snapshot every 50 ms; it waits until file identity, size, or modification time provides new evidence.

Missing, stale, incomplete, continuously changing, mismatched, timed-out, and canceled captures return no snapshot. The maximum wait remains three seconds.

## Legacy payloads keep the quiet-window fallback

When last_assistant_message is missing, null, or empty, Entire has no producer evidence that the current final response reached the transcript. It therefore retains the 500 ms quiet window used by older Claude Code versions.

The split is intentional:

| Payload | Readiness evidence | Timing behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modern | Stable owned snapshot, valid current-turn JSONL, final response match | Immediate first check; 50 ms polling only when not ready |
| Legacy | Stable owned snapshot, structurally valid ending, 500 ms without file changes | Always pays the quiet window |

## Repeatable Claude Stops remain refreshable

A blocking Claude Stop hook can cause the same assistant turn to continue and later emit another Stop without a new UserPromptSubmit event. A valid last_assistant_message proves readiness for one Stop; it does not prove that Claude will never continue afterward.

Claude therefore advertises a repeatable turn-end capability. After each Stop, Entire:

- finalizes checkpoints using the validated snapshot available at that Stop;
- retains the original turn boundary and checkpoint IDs;
- tracks commits made during a continuation; and
- refreshes the same checkpoints if another Stop arrives.

The next user prompt or SessionEnd seals the turn. stop_hook_active is preserved as protocol metadata but is not treated as proof that a Stop is permanently final.

If the latest checkpoint refresh fails, Entire keeps the last successfully stored transcript and preserves the checkpoint IDs as recovery bookkeeping. Successful session-end refreshes release those IDs; failed ones keep the supporting shadow-branch state protected from cleanup.

## File and token analysis share one parse

Claude file extraction and token calculation previously implemented separate capabilities, each of which parsed the same main transcript and subagent transcripts independently.

The optional TranscriptTurnAnalyzer capability now parses the current main turn once and derives both modified files and token usage from those records. Each subagent transcript is likewise parsed once for both results. Other agents retain the existing independent capability fallback.

Capture validation remains a separate, lightweight safety pass. Its question is whether the bytes are safe and complete; turn analysis answers what metadata those validated bytes contain.

## Capture and analysis timing

These are medians from three runs on an Apple M3. They measure transcript capture, validation, and transcript-backed metadata analysis, not complete end-to-end Stop-hook latency.

### Modern Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture + validation | File/token analysis | Total transcript latency |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB normal turn | 0.170 ms | 0.249 ms | 0.419 ms |
| 4 MiB large turn | 8.848 ms | 15.966 ms | 24.814 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small current turn at tail | 13.134 ms | 19.308 ms | 32.442 ms |
| 70 MiB entirely belonging to current turn | 152.057 ms | 281.803 ms | 433.860 ms |

The realistic large-history case is the third row: the transcript file is 70 MiB, but most records belong to earlier turns. The 433.860 ms case deliberately makes all 70 MiB one enormous current turn.

### Legacy Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture including quiet window | Analysis | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB | 501.098 ms | 0.249 ms | 501.347 ms |
| 4 MiB | 501.653 ms | 15.966 ms | 517.619 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small tail turn | 514.228 ms | 19.308 ms | 533.536 ms |
| 70 MiB full current turn | 514.228 ms | 281.803 ms | 796.031 ms |

Other timing cases:

- A modern transcript that is already ready has no artificial wait.
- If writing finishes after Stop begins, latency is the remaining write delay plus approximately 50–100 ms stability detection and processing time.
- A transcript that never becomes valid, or whose final response never matches, times out after three seconds.
- Missing or already stale transcripts fail immediately.

The common modern case moves from the previous PR design's unavoidable 50 ms first poll to actual processing time: under 1 ms for a small transcript and about 32 ms for a realistic 70 MiB historical session.

## Test coverage

Focused tests cover:

- immediate modern capture independent of the poll interval;
- legacy quiet-window behavior and mid-write pauses;
- repeated assistant text before the current-turn boundary;
- partial final JSON and complete JSON without a trailing newline;
- continued growth, truncation, replacement, and same-size rewrites with changed modification time;
- remembered rejection of an unchanged snapshot;
- missing, stale, timed-out, and canceled capture;
- source mutation after capture and finalization ownership;
- measured-zero versus unmeasured-zero turn positions;
- repeated Stops reusing one turn boundary;
- commits and checkpoint refreshes during Stop continuations; and
- successful versus failed session-end refresh cleanup.

The benchmarks live in cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/transcript_capture_test.go.

## Verification

Fresh verification for commit 40fbeb0c2:

- Required mise run check passed.
- Race-enabled unit and integration suite passed.
- Vogon canary passed 56/56.
- Roger-Roger canary passed 4/4.
- Post-commit mise run lint passed with 0 issues before push.
- git diff --check passed.

The separately reported test totals were:

- Unit: 9,740 tests, 5 skipped.
- Integration: 531 tests, 3 skipped.
- Lint: 0 issues.

## Kept out of this PR

This PR does not introduce a repository-wide TranscriptPreparer replacement, change external-agent readiness contracts, enforce a minimum Claude Code version, or claim end-to-end Stop-hook latency from the transcript-only benchmarks.

{"body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1095
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What

`redaction.openai_privacy_filter.command` becomes `argv[0]` of an `exec.CommandContext` call in the pre-push OPF rewrite, and it was read from the version-controlled `.entire/settings.json` with no validation. An ordinary pull request could pair a `command` with a payload committed alongside it and execute code on every developer who pushes.

Reported internally; I verified the whole chain and reproduced execution end-to-end before fixing.

## Why the existing controls didn't help

- The pre-push prompt never names the command it is about to run.
- `prompt_default: "always"` skips the prompt, and non-TTY pushes (CI, agent-driven) auto-run.
- Execution happens *before* any failure handling, so a payload exiting 0 with valid JSON leaves no warning at all.
- A JSON settings diff does not read as executable to a reviewer.

## The fix

The boundary is **ownership, not syntax** — a path is a legitimate setting for anyone whose `opf` binary isn't on `$PATH`, so banning paths would be a real regression.

1. **`command` is honored only from `.entire/settings.local.json`**, and only when that file is verified untracked.
2. **A tracked `settings.local.json` is ignored wholesale.** The filename is not the check: `.gitignore` does not apply to an already-tracked path, so `git add -f` commits it and a fresh clone materializes it with the committer's content. That file also silently overrides project settings for everyone, so this is a correctness fix as much as a security one.

Rejection is always a downgrade, never an error — one committed file must not brick `status` and `doctor`, the tools you'd use to diagnose it. `command` falls back to resolving `opf` on `$PATH`; if that's missing the rewrite fails closed rather than pushing content the user believed OPF had scanned.

### Two deliberate asymmetries

**Failure direction.** An unverifiable repository *keeps* the local layer (losing every local preference over an unreadable repo is worse than the risk) but still *drops* the exec-bearing command (being wrong there means running someone else's binary). No repository at all counts as positive proof of locality — nothing can arrive by cloning when there is nothing to clone.

1. **`command` is honored only from `.entire/settings.local.json`**, and only when that file is verified untracked.
2. **A tracked `settings.local.json` is ignored wholesale.** The filename is not the check: `.gitignore` does not apply to an already-tracked path, so `git add -f` commits it and a fresh clone materializes it with the committer's content. That file also silently overrides project settings for everyone, so this is a correctness fix as much as a security one.

Rejection is always a downgrade, never an error — one committed file must not brick `status` and `doctor`, the tools you'd use to diagnose it. `command` falls back to resolving `opf` on `$PATH`; if that's missing the rewrite fails closed rather than pushing content the user believed OPF had scanned.

### Two deliberate asymmetries

**Failure direction.** An unverifiable repository *keeps* the local layer (losing every local preference over an unreadable repo is worse than the risk) but still *drops* the exec-bearing command (being wrong there means running someone else's binary). No repository at all counts as positive proof of locality — nothing can arrive by cloning when there is nothing to clone.

**Check depth.** The layer check reads the git index; the `command` check also reads HEAD. A PR-delivered file is always in the index of a clone that checks it out, and checkout cannot produce a file absent from the index — so "committed then `git rm --cached`" is a state you created locally. HEAD is the expensive half and is reserved for the setting that gets executed.

## A deadlock this surfaced

Adding integration tests exposed a hard hang in the first version of the fix: `logging.Init` calls `logLevelGetter` — which loads settings, which logged — *while holding its own write lock*. Go's `RWMutex` isn't reentrant, so every hook froze in any repo carrying a project-level OPF command.

Fixed at the root by resolving the log level before taking the lock, which also makes the two pre-existing `logging.Debug` calls in `settings.Load` safe. `TestInit_GetterThatLogsDoesNotDeadlock` pins it — verified it hangs without the fix.

## Performance

The probe uses go-git rather than shelling out, and is memoized per process. `settings.Load` is uncached and runs ~5× per hook, so a naive implementation cost 15 subprocesses (+143ms) per hook. Measured per hook process, after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| this repo | 8.3ms | **2.5ms** |
| reftable repo | 39.3ms | **10.8ms** |

go-git also removes the dependency on `git` being on `$PATH` for ordinary repos — the GUI-git-client population, whose hooks don't inherit a shell profile, is exactly the group most likely to need an explicit `command` and would otherwise have silently lost it.

## Tests

21 unit + 3 integration. The integration tests run the real binary through real git hooks and include a **positive control** (same payload via an untracked local file *does* execute) — without it, "OPF never ran" would look identical to "OPF ran something safe".

Covered: project-file rejection, untracked-local happy path, staged, committed, committed-then-unstaged, tracked-local-wholesale, unverifiable repo, no repo, unborn/born HEAD, linked worktrees (own index), reftable, memoization + reset seam, and no-`git`-on-`$PATH`.

## Follow-ups not in this PR

- `agent/registry.go:34-43,65` has the same callback-under-lock shape as the logging deadlock, plus a recursive `RLock` via `List()` inside `Get()`. Latent today; it's a plugin extension point.
- `setup.go:650` writes a merged struct into a scoped settings file, which that file's own `saveEnabledState` comment forbids. Pre-existing, but it makes a rejected value lossy.
- Eight copies of `SetLogLevelGetter`+`Init` that `ensureCommandLogging` already exists to replace.
- A `doctor` check for the rejection — today it reaches stderr outside doctor's report format.
- A raw-byte index pre-filter would cut the probe 22× on very large repos (23ms → 0.86ms at 50k files), at the cost of index-format knowledge.

{"body":"Refs #2091, item 3 only.

Before this change, Claude Code's Stop hook waited for a transcript sentinel that no longer appears, then fell back to a 500 ms quiet window. The wait only validated a mutable path. Lifecycle copied that path later, and provisional-checkpoint finalization opened it once more. Entire could therefore store bytes other than the ones it had treated as ready.

This PR replaces that sequence with one owned, validated snapshot for Claude Stop. Modern Claude payloads provide the final assistant response, so Entire can validate a transcript immediately with no artificial wait. Older payloads retain the 500 ms quiet-window fallback. The lifecycle also keeps checkpoints refreshable across Claude's repeatable Stop events and derives file and token metadata from one transcript parse.

## The wait did not own the transcript

TranscriptPreparer returns only an error. It gives the caller no bytes, open handle, identity, size, or file version. A successful wait says that path state A looked ready, but lifecycle can then copy state B and checkpoint finalization can read state C.

Shortening the wait alone would reduce latency while leaving that race intact. Valid final JSON would not be enough either: a complete older prefix can be syntactically valid even when the current turn has not reached the file.

## Owned, validated Stop snapshots

The built-in Claude Code adapter now has a Stop-specific capture operation. It:

1. fingerprints the producer-owned transcript by file identity, size, and modification time;
2. reads exactly the observed byte range;
3. verifies both the opened handle and current path still identify the observed file version;
4. validates the JSONL and derives the position from those exact bytes; and
5. returns an Entire-owned snapshot used by lifecycle, metadata analysis, position advancement, and checkpoint finalization.

None of those consumers reopens Claude's live transcript for the same Stop. If the file changes during capture, the bytes are discarded and capture retries against the new version.

The portable fingerprint catches ordinary appends, truncation, replacement, and rewrites whose modification time changes. It cannot prove that a same-size rewrite did not happen when the filesystem also reports the same timestamp. Claude appends transcript records, so that is an acceptable limit here; the tests do not claim stronger detection.

## Modern readiness is evidence-based and immediate

For modern payloads, non-empty last_assistant_message supplies current-turn evidence. Capture requires a transcript position successfully measured at TurnStart, reconstructs the latest assistant text only after that boundary, and requires it to match Claude's supplied final response.

The first readiness check now runs immediately. The previous design waited for the first 50 ms ticker event even when the transcript was already complete. After the immediate attempt, incomplete captures return to the normal 50 ms polling cadence.

A rejected file fingerprint is remembered. Entire does not reread and revalidate the same unchanged 70 MiB snapshot every 50 ms; it waits until file identity, size, or modification time provides new evidence.

Missing, stale, incomplete, continuously changing, mismatched, timed-out, and canceled captures return no snapshot. The maximum wait remains three seconds.

## Legacy payloads keep the quiet-window fallback

When last_assistant_message is missing, null, or empty, Entire has no producer evidence that the current final response reached the transcript. It therefore retains the 500 ms quiet window used by older Claude Code versions.

The split is intentional:

| Payload | Readiness evidence | Timing behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modern | Stable owned snapshot, valid current-turn JSONL, final response match | Immediate first check; 50 ms polling only when not ready |
| Legacy | Stable owned snapshot, structurally valid ending, 500 ms without file changes | Always pays the quiet window |

## Repeatable Claude Stops remain refreshable

A blocking Claude Stop hook can cause the same assistant turn to continue and later emit another Stop without a new UserPromptSubmit event. A valid last_assistant_message proves readiness for one Stop; it does not prove that Claude will never continue afterward.

Claude therefore advertises a repeatable turn-end capability. After each Stop, Entire:

- finalizes checkpoints using the validated snapshot available at that Stop;
- retains the original turn boundary and checkpoint IDs;
- tracks commits made during a continuation; and
- refreshes the same checkpoints if another Stop arrives.

The next user prompt or SessionEnd seals the turn. stop_hook_active is preserved as protocol metadata but is not treated as proof that a Stop is permanently final.

If the latest checkpoint refresh fails, Entire keeps the last successfully stored transcript and preserves the checkpoint IDs as recovery bookkeeping. Successful session-end refreshes release those IDs; failed ones keep the supporting shadow-branch state protected from cleanup.

## File and token analysis share one parse

Claude file extraction and token calculation previously implemented separate capabilities, each of which parsed the same main transcript and subagent transcripts independently.

The optional TranscriptTurnAnalyzer capability now parses the current main turn once and derives both modified files and token usage from those records. Each subagent transcript is likewise parsed once for both results. Other agents retain the existing independent capability fallback.

Capture validation remains a separate, lightweight safety pass. Its question is whether the bytes are safe and complete; turn analysis answers what metadata those validated bytes contain.

## Capture and analysis timing

These are medians from three runs on an Apple M3. They measure transcript capture, validation, and transcript-backed metadata analysis, not complete end-to-end Stop-hook latency.

### Modern Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture + validation | File/token analysis | Total transcript latency |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB normal turn | 0.170 ms | 0.249 ms | 0.419 ms |
| 4 MiB large turn | 8.848 ms | 15.966 ms | 24.814 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small current turn at tail | 13.134 ms | 19.308 ms | 32.442 ms |
| 70 MiB entirely belonging to current turn | 152.057 ms | 281.803 ms | 433.860 ms |

The realistic large-history case is the third row: the transcript file is 70 MiB, but most records belong to earlier turns. The 433.860 ms case deliberately makes all 70 MiB one enormous current turn.

### Legacy Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture including quiet window | Analysis | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB | 501.098 ms | 0.249 ms | 501.347 ms |
| 4 MiB | 501.653 ms | 15.966 ms | 517.619 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small tail turn | 514.228 ms | 19.308 ms | 533.536 ms |
| 70 MiB full current turn | 514.228 ms | 281.803 ms | 796.031 ms |

Other timing cases:

- A modern transcript that is already ready has no artificial wait.
- If writing finishes after Stop begins, latency is the remaining write delay plus approximately 50–100 ms stability detection and processing time.
- A transcript that never becomes valid, or whose final response never matches, times out after three seconds.
- Missing or already stale transcripts fail immediately.

The common modern case moves from the previous PR design's unavoidable 50 ms first poll to actual processing time: under 1 ms for a small transcript and about 32 ms for a realistic 70 MiB historical session.

## Test coverage

Focused tests cover:

- immediate modern capture independent of the poll interval;
- legacy quiet-window behavior and mid-write pauses;
- repeated assistant text before the current-turn boundary;
- partial final JSON and complete JSON without a trailing newline;
- continued growth, truncation, replacement, and same-size rewrites with changed modification time;
- remembered rejection of an unchanged snapshot;
- missing, stale, timed-out, and canceled capture;
- source mutation after capture and finalization ownership;
- measured-zero versus unmeasured-zero turn positions;
- repeated Stops reusing one turn boundary;
- commits and checkpoint refreshes during Stop continuations; and
- successful versus failed session-end refresh cleanup.

The benchmarks live in cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/transcript_capture_test.go.

## Verification

Fresh verification for commit 40fbeb0c2:

- Required mise run check passed.
- Race-enabled unit and integration suite passed.
- Vogon canary passed 56/56.
- Roger-Roger canary passed 4/4.
- Post-commit mise run lint passed with 0 issues before push.
- git diff --check passed.

The separately reported test totals were:

- Unit: 9,740 tests, 5 skipped.
- Integration: 531 tests, 3 skipped.
- Lint: 0 issues.

## Kept out of this PR

This PR does not introduce a repository-wide TranscriptPreparer replacement, change external-agent readiness contracts, enforce a minimum Claude Code version, or claim end-to-end Stop-hook latency from the transcript-only benchmarks.

145	// ParseHookEvent translates a Pi hook invocation into a normalised lifecycle
   146	// event. Implements agent.HookSupport.
   147	func (a *PiAgent) ParseHookEvent(ctx context.Context, hookName string, stdin io.Reader) (*agent.Event, error) {
   148		// Stream one JSON value rather than io.ReadAll so the hook never blocks
   149		// waiting for stdin EOF that some agents don't send on Windows (issue #1398).
   150		parsed, err := agent.ReadAndParseHookInput[piHookPayload](stdin)
   151		if err != nil {
   152			return nil, err
   153		}
   154		payload := *parsed
   155	
   156		sessionID := payload.SessionID
   157		if sessionID == "" {
   158			sessionID = extractSessionIDFromPath(payload.SessionFile)
   159		}
   160	
   161		now := time.Now()
   162	
   163		// A sessionless payload names no session we can track, and must not be resolved
   164		// against the per-repo session-ID cache: doing so handed the caller whichever
   165		// session happened to be cached — see docs/architecture/agent-guide.md for how a
   166		// nested `pi --no-session` subagent thereby claimed its parent's session.
   167		//
   168		// session_shutdown is exempt: the extension sends it with no session identity at
   169		// all, and it must still clear the cache. Same shape as Copilot CLI's
   170		// subordinate-session guard (copilotcli/lifecycle.go).
   171		if hookName != HookNameSessionShutdown && sessionID == "" {
   172			logging.Debug(ctx, "pi: skipping lifecycle event for sessionless (nested) Pi invocation",
   173				slog.String("hook", hookName))
   174			return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // Sessionless/nested Pi — no session to track.
   175		}
   176	
   177		switch hookName {
   178		case HookNameSessionStart:
   179			cacheSessionID(ctx, sessionID)
   180			return &agent.Event{
   181				Type:      agent.SessionStart,
   182				SessionID: sessionID,
   183				Timestamp: now,
   184			}, nil
   185	
   186		case HookNameBeforeAgentStart:
   187			cacheSessionID(ctx, sessionID)
   188			// Provide the live Pi session file as SessionRef so state.TranscriptPath
   189			// is populated before any mid-turn commits. Without this, the
   190			// post-commit hook cannot condense when no shadow branch exists yet.
   191			return &agent.Event{
   192				Type:        agent.TurnStart,
   193				SessionID:   sessionID,
   194				SessionRef:  payload.SessionFile,
   195				Prompt:      payload.Prompt,
   196				Timestamp:   now,
   197				SkillEvents: piSkillEvents(payload.SkillEvents),
   198			}, nil
   199	
   200		case HookNameAgentEnd:
   201			// Capture the Pi JSONL into <repo>/.entire/tmp/pi/<id>.json so the
   202			// strategy has a stable transcript reference even if the user later
   203			// deletes Pi sessions. The pi/ subdir avoids colliding with paths
   204			// other agents (or test harnesses) stage under .entire/tmp/.
   205			sessionRef := captureTranscript(ctx, sessionID, payload.SessionFile)
   206			return &agent.Event{
   207				Type:       agent.TurnEnd,
   208				SessionID:  sessionID,
   209				SessionRef: sessionRef,
   210				Model:      extractModelFromPiSessionFile(sessionRef),
   211				Timestamp:  now,
   212			}, nil
   213	
   214		case HookNameSessionShutdown:
   215			// Cleanup-only: clear the cached session ID. We intentionally do NOT
   216			// emit SessionEnd here.
   217			//
   218			// Pi fires session_shutdown and agent_end on session teardown, and the
   219			// TypeScript extension dispatches both via separate `entire hooks pi …`
   220			// child processes (execFile is non-blocking). Child-process startup
   221			// ordering then decides which event reaches the lifecycle dispatcher
   222			// first; if session_shutdown wins, an emitted SessionEnd transitions
   223			// the session to "ended" before agent_end can save the linkable
   224			// checkpoint, leaving prepare-commit-msg with no session to attach a
   225			// trailer to and the user's commit unlinked.
   226			//
   227			// agent_end is the source of truth for "turn complete" (and, for Pi,
   228			// effectively "session over" for any single-turn `pi -p` invocation).
   229			// SessionEnd is left for the framework to derive from idle timeout or
   230			// the next SessionStart's stale-state cleanup.
   231			clearCachedSessionID(ctx)
   232			return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // intentional: cleanup-only, no lifecycle event
   233	
   234		default:
   235			// Unknown / future hooks have no lifecycle significance.
   236			return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // unknown hook = no lifecycle event (acceptable)
   237		}
   238	}
   239	
   240	// --- session ID cache ---
   240	// --- session ID cache ---
   241	//
   242	// This cached the active session ID so a later hook arriving without one could
   243	// recover it. The sessionless guard in ParseHookEvent removed the only two reads:
   244	// a payload with no resolvable session ID is now skipped rather than resolved
   245	// against this file, because the file is a single per-repo slot and handing its
   246	// contents to an unrelated caller is what let a nested subagent claim its parent's
   247	// session.
   248	//
   249	// The recovery it promised was never reachable anyway — a payload with no session
   250	// file also has no transcript, so captureTranscript returns "" and the event dies
   251	// downstream regardless of the ID.

   166		// nested `pi --no-session` subagent thereby claimed its parent's session.

   169		// all, and it must still clear the cache. Same shape as Copilot CLI's
   170		// subordinate-session guard (copilotcli/lifecycle.go).

   186		case HookNameBeforeAgentStart:

   191			return &agent.Event{

   193				SessionID:   sessionID,

    25	// partitionLocalRefs splits refs into those that exist locally (pushable) and
    26	// those that don't (stale queue entries — e.g. a checkpoint ref deleted by
    27	// cleanup). Stale refs can never push, so callers drop them from the queue
    28	// rather than retrying them forever.
    29	func partitionLocalRefs(repo *git.Repository, refs []plumbing.ReferenceName) (existing, stale []plumbing.ReferenceName) {
    30		for _, ref := range refs {
    31			_, err := repo.Reference(ref, false)
    32			switch {
    33			case err == nil:
    34				existing = append(existing, ref)
    35			case errors.Is(err, plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound):
    36				// Genuinely gone (e.g. deleted by cleanup) — never pushable, drop it.
    37				stale = append(stale, ref)
    38			default:
    39				// A transient/IO lookup error: keep the ref as pushable so a real
    40				// entry isn't dropped from the queue forever over a flaky read.
    41				existing = append(existing, ref)
    42			}
    43		}
    44		return existing, stale
    45	}
    46	
    47	// batchPushRefs pushes all of refs to target in a single git push,
    48	// fast-forward-only (NOT a force push). Batching keeps a backfill of many refs to
    49	// one network round-trip. Per-checkpoint refs normally advance by fast-forward
    50	// (each write parents on the prior tip), so the common case succeeds; a
    51	// non-fast-forward update — genuine divergence, e.g. the same checkpoint written
    52	// differently on another machine — is REJECTED rather than silently overwriting
    53	// the remote. We deliberately do not force: there is no server-side ref
    54	// protection, so a force push would make a buggy or racing client clobber good
    55	// remote history with no signal. On rejection the whole push errors; the caller
    56	// retries the rejected refs individually with fetch+replay recovery
    57	// (pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery).
    58	func batchPushRefs(ctx context.Context, target string, refs []plumbing.ReferenceName) error {
    59		if len(refs) == 0 {
    60			return nil
    61		}
    62		refSpecs := make([]string, 0, len(refs))
    63		for _, ref := range refs {
    64			refSpecs = append(refSpecs, ref.String()+":"+ref.String())
    65		}
    66		if _, err := remote.PushWithOptions(ctx, remote.PushOptions{Remote: target, RefSpecs: refSpecs}); err != nil {

    68		}

    75	// commits on top via fetchAndRebaseRefCommon, then retries. The retry is still
    76	// non-force: after the replay the local ref is a fast-forward over the remote, so

    22		"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing/object"
    23	)
    24	
    25	// partitionLocalRefs splits refs into those that exist locally (pushable) and
    26	// those that don't (stale queue entries — e.g. a checkpoint ref deleted by
    27	// cleanup). Stale refs can never push, so callers drop them from the queue
    28	// rather than retrying them forever.
    29	func partitionLocalRefs(repo *git.Repository, refs []plumbing.ReferenceName) (existing, stale []plumbing.ReferenceName) {
    30		for _, ref := range refs {
    31			_, err := repo.Reference(ref, false)
    32			switch {
    33			case err == nil:
    34				existing = append(existing, ref)
    35			case errors.Is(err, plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound):
    36				// Genuinely gone (e.g. deleted by cleanup) — never pushable, drop it.
    37				stale = append(stale, ref)
    38			default:
    39				// A transient/IO lookup error: keep the ref as pushable so a real
    40				// entry isn't dropped from the queue forever over a flaky read.
    41				existing = append(existing, ref)
    42			}
    43		}
    44		return existing, stale
    45	}
    46	
    47	// batchPushRefs pushes all of refs to target in a single git push,
    48	// fast-forward-only (NOT a force push). Batching keeps a backfill of many refs to
    49	// one network round-trip. Per-checkpoint refs normally advance by fast-forward
    50	// (each write parents on the prior tip), so the common case succeeds; a
    51	// non-fast-forward update — genuine divergence, e.g. the same checkpoint written
    52	// differently on another machine — is REJECTED rather than silently overwriting
    53	// the remote. We deliberately do not force: there is no server-side ref
    54	// protection, so a force push would make a buggy or racing client clobber good
    55	// remote history with no signal. On rejection the whole push errors; the caller
    56	// retries the rejected refs individually with fetch+replay recovery
    57	// (pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery).
    58	func batchPushRefs(ctx context.Context, target string, refs []plumbing.ReferenceName) error {
    59		if len(refs) == 0 {
    60			return nil
    61		}
    62		refSpecs := make([]string, 0, len(refs))
    63		for _, ref := range refs {
    64			refSpecs = append(refSpecs, ref.String()+":"+ref.String())
    65		}
    66		if _, err := remote.PushWithOptions(ctx, remote.PushOptions{Remote: target, RefSpecs: refSpecs}); err != nil {
    67			return fmt.Errorf("push %d checkpoint refs: %w", len(refs), err)
    68		}
    69		return nil
    70	}
    71	
    72	// pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery pushes a single checkpoint ref fast-forward-only;
    73	// on rejection — typically the ref diverged on the remote (the same checkpoint
    74	// re-written elsewhere) — it fetches the remote ref and replays the local-only
    75	// commits on top via fetchAndRebaseRefCommon, then retries. The retry is still
    76	// non-force: after the replay the local ref is a fast-forward over the remote, so
    77	// the remote commit is preserved as an ancestor rather than overwritten. The
    78	// cherry-pick is delta-based, so non-overlapping changes merge; a genuine overlap
    79	// (e.g. both sides rewrote the root metadata.json) surfaces as a rebase error and
    80	// the ref is left for a later pre-push. Returns nil only if the ref reached the
    81	// remote.
    82	func pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery(ctx context.Context, target string, ref plumbing.ReferenceName) error {
    83		// One shared budget across the initial push, fetch+replay, and retry, matching
    84		// doPushRef (fetchAndRebaseRefCommon relies on the caller's deadline).
    85		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, checkpointPushBudget)
    86		defer cancel()
    87	
    88		if err := batchPushRefs(ctx, target, []plumbing.ReferenceName{ref}); err == nil {
    89			return nil
    90		}
    91		if err := fetchAndRebaseRefCommon(ctx, target, ref); err != nil {
    92			return fmt.Errorf("sync diverged checkpoint ref %s: %w", ref, err)
    93		}
    94		return batchPushRefs(ctx, target, []plumbing.ReferenceName{ref})
    95	}
    96	
    97	// pushRefIfNeeded pushes a ref to the given target if it has unpushed changes.
    98	// The target can be a remote name (e.g., "origin") or a URL for direct push.
    99	// For branch refs, the "has unpushed" optimization consults the remote-tracking
   100	// ref. Non-branch refs and URL targets skip the optimization and let git
   101	// handle the no-op case.
   102	// Does not check any settings — callers are responsible for gating.
   103	func pushRefIfNeeded(ctx context.Context, target string, ref plumbing.ReferenceName) (delivered bool, err error) {
   104		repo, err := OpenRepository(ctx)
   105		if err != nil {
   106			logging.Debug(ctx, "push skipped: open repository failed",
   107				slog.String("ref", ref.String()),
   108				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
   109			return false, nil
   110		}

   109

   114		testutil.GitAdd(t, workDir, "two.txt")

   126	// rejected, and the remote ref is left untouched — the safety property that
   127	// distinguishes this from a force push (we have no server-side ref protection).
   128	func TestBatchPushRefs_RejectsNonFastForward(t *testing.T) {
   129		workDir, bareDir, refs := setupRepoWithCheckpointRefs(t)
   130		t.Chdir(workDir)
   131		ctx := context.Background()
   132

   134		original := remoteRefHash(t, bareDir, refs[0])

   137		// pushed, so the update is non-fast-forward.
   138		runGit := func(args ...string) string {

   140			c.Dir = workDir
   141			c.Env = testutil.GitIsolatedEnv()

   182

   185		testutil.GitAdd(t, workDir, "b.txt")
   186		testutil.GitCommit(t, workDir, "add b")

    10	// CheckpointReadRemotes returns the ordered, deduped remotes that checkpoint
    11	// READS consult: the elected sync remote first, then "origin" as the legacy
    12	// tier (pre-single-remote-sync checkpoints live there, and a fresh clone
    13	// may lack the local settings that elected a non-origin remote).
    14	//
    15	// Unlike the write-side election, this fails OPEN: on an election error
    16	// (misconfigured checkpoint_push_remote, unreadable settings) the chain is
    17	// ["origin"] when configured. Writes fail closed to prevent leaking data;
    18	// failing reads closed would only prevent FINDING data, with no privacy
    19	// benefit. Callers must uphold the read-only rule for every candidate after
    20	// the first: only the elected remote may seed or advance local refs.
    21	//
    22	// An empty result means no candidates — callers needing the "checkpoint
    23	// absent" classification must gather their own positive evidence (successful
    24	// remote listing, readable settings); an empty chain alone is not proof.
    25	//
    26	// The election itself is deliberately un-memoized: every call re-runs it, so a
    27	// settings change or a captured election written mid-invocation is observed
    28	// immediately. What IS memoized, per invocation, are the two .git/config reads
    29	// underneath it — which remotes exist, and does remote X exist (see
    30	// git_remote_cache.go). That split is load-bearing: caching the election result
    31	// would make #1991's capture invisible to the gate that runs right after it.
    32	func CheckpointReadRemotes(ctx context.Context) []string {
    33		return CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx).Candidates
    34	}
    35	
    36	// CheckpointReadResolution is the read-candidate chain bundled with the
    37	// election result it was derived from.
    38	type CheckpointReadResolution struct {
    39		// Candidates is the ordered read-candidate chain (see
    40		// CheckpointReadRemotes).
    41		Candidates []string
    42		// ElectedName is the elected checkpoint sync remote; "" when the election
    43		// failed or elected nothing. Only this remote may seed or advance local
    44		// refs.
    45		ElectedName string
    46		// ElectionErr records a failed election. It is advisory for readers (the
    47		// chain fail-opens to ["origin"] when configured); write-adjacent callers
    48		// may surface it when they need a push target.
    49		ElectionErr error
    50	}
    51	
    52	// CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection returns the read-candidate chain together
    53	// with the election result it was derived from, so callers that need both —
    54	// e.g. to confine local-ref advancement to the elected remote while iterating
    55	// the chain — make ONE election call instead of two that could disagree if
    56	// settings or remotes change mid-operation. See CheckpointReadRemotes for the
    57	// read-side fail-open rationale and cost note.
    58	func CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx context.Context) CheckpointReadResolution {
    59		var res CheckpointReadResolution
    60		elected, err := ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)
    61		switch {
    62		case err != nil:
    63			res.ElectionErr = err
    64			logging.Debug(ctx, "checkpoint reads: election failed, falling back to origin only",
    65				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
    66		case elected.Name != "":
    67			res.ElectedName = elected.Name
    68			res.Candidates = append(res.Candidates, elected.Name)
    69		}
    70		if isConfiguredRemote(ctx, "origin") && (len(res.Candidates) == 0 || res.Candidates[0] != "origin") {
    71			res.Candidates = append(res.Candidates, "origin")
    72		}
    73		return res
    74	}

    25	// partitionLocalRefs splits refs into those that exist locally (pushable) and
    26	// those that don't (stale queue entries — e.g. a checkpoint ref deleted by
    27	// cleanup). Stale refs can never push, so callers drop them from the queue

    29	func partitionLocalRefs(repo *git.Repository, refs []plumbing.ReferenceName) (existing, stale []plumbing.ReferenceName) {
    30		for _, ref := range refs {
    31			_, err := repo.Reference(ref, false)
    32			switch {
    33			case err == nil:
    34				existing = append(existing, ref)
    35			case errors.Is(err, plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound):
    36				// Genuinely gone (e.g. deleted by cleanup) — never pushable, drop it.
    37				stale = append(stale, ref)
    38			default:
    39				// A transient/IO lookup error: keep the ref as pushable so a real
    40				// entry isn't dropped from the queue forever over a flaky read.
    41				existing = append(existing, ref)
    42			}
    43		}
    44		return existing, stale
    45	}

    47	// batchPushRefs pushes all of refs to target in a single git push,
    48	// fast-forward-only (NOT a force push). Batching keeps a backfill of many refs to
    49	// one network round-trip. Per-checkpoint refs normally advance by fast-forward
    50	// (each write parents on the prior tip), so the common case succeeds; a
    51	// non-fast-forward update — genuine divergence, e.g. the same checkpoint written
    52	// differently on another machine — is REJECTED rather than silently overwriting
    53	// the remote. We deliberately do not force: there is no server-side ref
    54	// protection, so a force push would make a buggy or racing client clobber good

    56	// retries the rejected refs individually with fetch+replay recovery
    57	// (pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery).
    58	func batchPushRefs(ctx context.Context, target string, refs []plumbing.ReferenceName) error {
    59		if len(refs) == 0 {

    12	// tier (pre-single-remote-sync checkpoints live there, and a fresh clone

    16	// (misconfigured checkpoint_push_remote, unreadable settings) the chain is
    17	// ["origin"] when configured. Writes fail closed to prevent leaking data;
    18	// failing reads closed would only prevent FINDING data, with no privacy
    19	// benefit. Callers must uphold the read-only rule for every candidate after
    20	// the first: only the elected remote may seed or advance local refs.
    21	//
    22	// An empty result means no candidates — callers needing the "checkpoint
    23	// absent" classification must gather their own positive evidence (successful
    24	// remote listing, readable settings); an empty chain alone is not proof.
    25	//
    26	// The election itself is deliberately un-memoized: every call re-runs it, so a
    27	// settings change or a captured election written mid-invocation is observed
    28	// immediately. What IS memoized, per invocation, are the two .git/config reads
    29	// underneath it — which remotes exist, and does remote X exist (see
    30	// git_remote_cache.go). That split is load-bearing: caching the election result
    31	// would make #1991's capture invisible to the gate that runs right after it.
    32	func CheckpointReadRemotes(ctx context.Context) []string {
    33		return CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx).Candidates

    36	// CheckpointReadResolution is the read-candidate chain bundled with the
    37	// election result it was derived from.
    38	type CheckpointReadResolution struct {
    39		// Candidates is the ordered read-candidate chain (see
    40		// CheckpointReadRemotes).
    41		Candidates []string
    42		// ElectedName is the elected checkpoint sync remote; "" when the election
    43		// failed or elected nothing. Only this remote may seed or advance local
    44		// refs.
    45		ElectedName string
    46		// ElectionErr records a failed election. It is advisory for readers (the
    47		// chain fail-opens to ["origin"] when configured); write-adjacent callers
    48		// may surface it when they need a push target.
    49		ElectionErr error
    50	}
    51	
    52	// CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection returns the read-candidate chain together
    53	// with the election result it was derived from, so callers that need both —
    54	// e.g. to confine local-ref advancement to the elected remote while iterating
    55	// the chain — make ONE election call instead of two that could disagree if
    56	// settings or remotes change mid-operation. See CheckpointReadRemotes for the
    57	// read-side fail-open rationale and cost note.
    58	func CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx context.Context) CheckpointReadResolution {

    64			logging.Debug(ctx, "checkpoint reads: election failed, falling back to origin only",
    65				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
    66		case elected.Name != "":
    67			res.ElectedName = elected.Name
    68			res.Candidates = append(res.Candidates, elected.Name)
    69		}

content.text:
I reviewed 235 unique `entireio/cli` PRs from August 10–31, 2026: 224 created during the window plus 11 older PRs closed during it. I also checked the proposed follow-ups against latest `upstream/main` at `486de6900`.

No files were changed.

## What the team is mainly working on

| Area | PRs mentioning area | Main work |
|---|---:|---|
| Checkpoints and sessions | 91 | Transcript durability, shadow checkpoints, git-refs, condensation, tokens, attach/import/resume |
| Agents and hooks | 78 | Claude, Cursor, Codex, Pi, Grok, external agents, hook reliability |
| Tests and tooling | 63 | E2E reliability, test isolation, installers, CI, logging |
| Cloud/auth/routing | 30 | Cells, jurisdictions, cluster auth, remotes, mirrors |
| Search/review/dispatch | 23 | Search UX, review execution, dispatch routing |
| Settings/configuration | 21 | Local/project settings, enable/disable, trust boundaries |
| Security/privacy/filesystem | 19 | Redaction, symlinks, filesystem confinement, credential safety |
| Explicit performance work | 15 | Batching, caching, reduced transcript parsing, fewer subprocesses |

These categories overlap. Of the 235 PRs, 87 are explicitly bug fixes, compared with 46 features and 10 explicitly labelled performance changes.

The dominant bug patterns are:

- Silent or partial checkpoint-data loss.
- Hook latency, cancellation, and subprocess lifetime.
- Wrong remote/cell/auth target selection.
- Transcript-shape drift between agent versions.
- Tests accidentally reading developer configuration or launching real tools.
- Platform-specific paths, symlinks, Windows and WSL behavior.
- Redaction and untrusted-input boundaries.
- Misleading success/error messages.

## Prioritized small bugs

### 1. Prevent merged settings from leaking across scopes

Priority: Highest  
Estimated files: 2 — `setup.go`, `setup_test.go`  
Status: Ready; no competing PR found

Merged PR [#2056](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2056) explicitly identified this follow-up. The bug remains in [current `setup.go`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/486de690083a6c69d10aa42bdeab26b3aac0d283/cmd/entire/cli/setup.go#L640-L658):

1. Adding an external agent calls `LoadEntireSettings`, producing the merged project+local view.
2. It changes `ExternalAgents`.
3. It writes that entire merged object to either `settings.json` or `settings.local.json`.

This can copy local-only paths, log settings, strategy options, or checkpoint-remote preferences into committed project settings.

Suggested title:

`fix(setup): keep external_agents writes scoped to their settings file`

Acceptance criteria:

- Only `external_agents` changes in the selected file.
- Existing fields in that file survive unchanged.
- Fields from the other settings scope are not copied.
- Tests cover local → project and project → local contamination.

This is the best high-value, reviewable bug.

---

### 2. Implement Cursor’s tool-invocation scanner

Priority: High  
Estimated files: 2 — `agent/cursor/transcript.go`, `transcript_test.go`  
Status: Ready; no competing PR found

Merged PR [#2120](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2120) confirmed that Cursor records:

```text
tool: Shell
input key: command
```

Its PR description explicitly says this resolves the blocker for `ToolInvocationScanner`. Nevertheless, current main still contains [`TestCursorAgent_MustNotImplementToolInvocationScanner`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/486de690083a6c69d10aa42bdeab26b3aac0d283/cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/transcript_test.go#L224-L241).

Impact: Cursor sessions remain “unsupported” for structured search-usage detection even though the checked-in real-session fixture contains everything needed.

Suggested title:

`fix(cursor): scan structured tool invocations from transcripts`

Acceptance criteria:

- `CursorAgent` implements `agent.ToolInvocationScanner`.
- `Shell.input.command` populates `ToolInvocation.Command`.
- Write/read tool calls expose their tool names.
- Hints remain a performance filter, not a semantic filter.
- Malformed lines fail open.
- The existing real Cursor fixture proves the mapping.
- Avoid copying Claude’s private walker wholesale; use Cursor’s existing transcript types to avoid duplication.

This is a good agent-integration task with concrete fixtures and no real-agent E2E requirement.

---

### 3. Make `attach` suggest the remote it actually searched

Priority: High, but very small  
Estimated files: 2 — `attach.go`, `attach_test.go`  
Status: Ready; no competing PR found

Merged PR [#1951](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1951) records a known cosmetic residual. Current [attach code](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/486de690083a6c69d10aa42bdeab26b3aac0d283/cmd/entire/cli/attach.go#L641-L649) admits that attach may search the elected checkpoint remote but print:

```text
git fetch origin ...
```

The suggested command therefore may not retrieve the missing checkpoint.

Suggested title:

`fix(attach): name the elected checkpoint remote in fetch hints`
